program: Older adult home modification and housing stability

what: North West Housing Partnership helps suburban Chicago homeowners repair homes and navigate housing decisions.
Its older adult program combines occupational therapy, nursing and contractor-installed safety modifications.
Accessible homes can help older residents manage daily activities and remain independent.
strengths: A current local program addresses concrete accessibility barriers.
Randomized CAPABLE evidence supports a short-term functional mechanism in some populations.
Home changes can plausibly protect household resources as well as independence.
reservations: Current annual completions, local utility gains and additional household savings are unverified.
HUD funding and municipal alternatives weaken an unrestricted donation counterfactual.
Trial results are mixed, while full outside resource costs and marginal capacity remain unknown.

sections.what: North West Housing Partnership, EIN 36-3715417, provides housing repair, development and counseling in the Chicago metropolitan area. Current OAHMP eligibility covers homeowners aged 62 or older in Cook, DuPage, Lake, Kane and McHenry counties. Occupational therapists and registered nurses guide contractor-installed modifications. The official support page solicits donations; no checkout transaction was performed.
sections.monitoring: A primary HUD bulletin reports an August 2023 $800,000 award for planned modifications in 75 units. This is a multi-period plan, not 75 verified current annual completions. The current program page establishes a free, HUD-funded service and assessment process, not a deduplicated annual cohort, completed dose, control group or new-donation bottleneck. Municipal and AgeOptions services remain relevant alternatives. The numerical 100 annual opportunities, 0.5 additional funded-work response and 0.6 clinical completion/fidelity are judgments. Cases use 75 opportunities or 25 per year if the historical plan were spread across three years; neither is observed current throughput.
sections.qualitative: The 2019 CAPABLE randomized trial tested up to ten OT, nurse and home-modifier visits over five months in 300 low-income Baltimore residents aged at least 65. The adjusted ADL ratio was 0.70 at five months; the 12-month ratio was 0.90 with a confidence interval including no effect. In the 2025 posthospital trial of 268 adults, overall ADL improvement was not significant, although mobility improved. Local OT/RN involvement does not establish equivalent dose, baseline disability or fidelity. Neither study measures a transferable 0.03 QALY increment, avoided injurious falls, mortality or local household savings. The clinical center retains the original weak utility judgment for a finite five months, not an empirically calibrated estimate. Nonrandomized Medicare expenditure estimates concern payer spending, not household cash or validated social resource savings.
sections.cost:
FY2025 original expense is $642,680; FY2024 is $542,871. FY2023 $902,809 expense plus $729,996 separately netted inventory cost gives $1,632,805 full recognized cost. Schedule D's $390,852 reconciliation is already included, not added twice. FY2024 minus $1 donated-service reconciliation is immaterial, not meaningful negative resources. FY2023 rental gross and net match in retrieved fields; absence of an addback is not proof of zero resources. Three-year mean is $939,452; property activity makes it imperfect operating comparison. Unrecognized volunteer and outside resources remain unknown.

Judged 100 local household opportunities and .5 additional annual-work response expose 50 households. Completion .6 yields 30 clinical residents within that union. Judged .03 utility for five months, quarter-year delay and 3% discount give .372239 clinical QALYs. Whole annual cost remains; this is a narrow conditional channel, not full portfolio or measured marginal-gift productivity.

Fifteen households conditionally avoid $1,000 actual repair spending and $500 net energy/care burdens in one year, net of taxes, benefits, replacement support and maintenance. Each positive component retains .5 for health overlap; negative components remain full. Full $100 disruption/time cost leaves $650. Thirty-five others lose $100. At $25,000 annual resources and one welfare-equivalent person per household, one joint log yields .121467 equivalents. Additional family welfare is unpriced. Combined .493706 gives $13.017467 million per ten combined equivalents, not ten clinical QALYs.

Resource exposure and costs survive clinical failure. Full 50-household harm and distinct local payer/contractor losses are stresses. Central outside incidence and harms are unknown-neutral, not observed zero or complete-world benefit. Public and nonlocal opportunity costs remain unpriced.

Deep review keeps the original central price unchanged: $13.017467 million per ten combined healthy-year welfare equivalents, comprising 0.372239 clinical QALYs and 0.121467 income equivalents. Income equivalents are not clinical QALYs. The apparent precision comes from arithmetic, not empirical calibration. One modeled welfare-equivalent person per household excludes additional family effects. Fifty household opportunities form the full exposed union; thirty clinical residents are a subset. Resource success among fifteen households is independent of clinical success, and burdens survive a clinical null.

The $1,000 avoided repair spending must be cash the household would actually have paid absent NWHP after HUD, municipal and other support—not retail repair value or property appreciation. The $500 energy/care gain is already net of replacement services; distinct tax, benefit-withdrawal, work and maintenance parameters test missing incidence without asserting observations. Positive components alone receive the overlap haircut before being combined with full negative components and full burdens in one household log. The default one-year resource horizon is finite; extended-horizon cases repeat only energy/care/work changes, benefit withdrawal and maintenance. Repair spending avoided and process disruption are one-off in the first year. Zero resource duration removes gains but keeps full one-off process burden. Counterparty stresses price lost contractor margin or displaced public beneficiaries as distinct households. Those stresses do not double-charge donation expenditure already in the full annual denominator. Nonlocal and whole-portfolio incidence remain unknown; a positive partial ledger is not complete-world benefit.
sections.funding: The original fiscal 2025 Form 990 reports $642,680 recognized expenses and $122,697 government grants. FY2024 gross cost is $542,871; FY2023 includes $902,809 expenses plus $729,996 separately netted inventory cost, totaling $1,632,805. Schedule D's $390,852 reconciliation is already in the 990 expense. The three-year mean is $939,452, but property activity makes it an imperfect recurring operating comparator. The FY2024 minus $1 reconciliation is an immaterial presentation oddity, not negative social resources. The HUD $800,000 award is neither an additional FY2025 expense nor proof of an unfunded current cohort. Whole-recipient annual cost is compared with a limited local channel; the 0.5 response is a conditional annual-work counterfactual, not a measured next-gift multiplier. Marginal donations, public-funding replacement and volunteer capacity require direct follow-up.

model.geographicAttribution: Chicago metro households; clinical residents are a subset of resource exposure.
model.formula: Health = N × b × completion × q × discounted finite health years minus full exposed-union harms. Household resources = 0.5 × disjoint household units × discounted years × log(1 + jointly net signed resources / baseline). Positive overlap applies to each positive component only. Headline = 10 × full annual recognized cost plus separately identified external economic cost / (clinical QALYs + resource equivalents). Repair savings and process costs occur once. Recurring resources and maintenance share one first-year net log and separate later-year joint logs; zero resource duration retains process costs.
model.counterfactual: Existing HUD-funded, municipal and AgeOptions services continue; some households would defer repairs or not purchase them. Conditional annual work adds only incremental outcomes beyond those alternatives. Next-gift response and full portfolio effects remain unknown.
model.attribution: Throughput, additional annual response, completion, utility and actual spending are separate judgments.
model.uncertainty: Conditional original priors retained, not empirically calibrated whole-portfolio expected value. Local cohorts, trial transfer, actual otherwise-paid spending, household baseline and public-resource replacement are unknown. Unknown controls remain null, not factual zero.
model.nativeOutcomes: Additional completed home modifications and short-term functional independence, plus actual net household spending avoided; not announced units, repair retail value, property wealth or payer expenditure counted as household income.
